query: What's new in health and medicine?
summary:
Recent discussions in health and medicine have focused on the effectiveness and value of over-the-counter cold and flu medications. A report from BBC highlights that many consumers may be overpaying for "max strength" cold and flu pills, as experts suggest that there is little difference in efficacy between these premium products and cheaper alternatives. Professor Jayne Lawrence from the University of Manchester emphasizes that basic painkillers are often just as effective, and consumers might benefit from opting for less expensive options that have also been tested for safety and effectiveness [Are max strength cold and flu pills worth the money?].

The article points out that while well-known brands may provide reassurance to shoppers, the actual performance of these medications does not significantly differ from their lower-cost counterparts. This insight comes at a time when many individuals are seeking relief during the flu season, prompting a reevaluation of spending on health products [Are max strength cold and flu pills worth the money?].

Overall, the findings suggest a need for consumers to be more discerning about their choices in cold and flu remedies, potentially leading to cost savings without sacrificing health outcomes. However, the articles do not provide new developments in other areas of health and medicine beyond this discussion on cold and flu medications.

Image source, Getty Images By Jim Reed Health reporter Published 43 minutes ago Your throat's painful, your head throbs and your blocked nose has kept you awake all night. It's that time of year again - flu season - and you'll try anything to feel normal. But is that pricey max strength flu remedy really any better than a basic box of painkillers? "The big brands have been around for a while, they've been tested, and there are adverts on the TV saying they're really good," says Prof Jayne Lawrence, head of the pharmacy division at the University of Manchester. "But in reality, there's very little difference. Personally, I'd always go for the cheaper ones - and they’ve also been tested." article_hits.content: Entering into the world of venture capital has never been easy, especially as a first-time fund manager. But it’s especially daunting right now. According to PitchBook data, firms raising their fourth fund “or later” captured a whopping 88.2% of U.S. VC fundraising dollars through the first three quarters of this year, while first-time funds captured a measly 4.5% . Just 81 first-time funds closed in the first nine months of 2026. That puts the year on track to be the worst for first-time managers in at least a decade, according to PitchBook’s estimate. Olaf Sakkers has spent the past five years proving that difficult doesn’t mean impossible. He founded his firm RedBlue Capital in 2021 and closed its first fund with roughly $5 million in capital commitments in 2023. He has now held a first close on a second fund that he says will total at least $50 million. article_hits.content: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China.
